lead: A busbar is a thick metal bar that takes power from a source and hands it to a group of loads. How generators are joined to the busbars — split, parallel or split-parallel — decides whether one fault darkens one bus or the whole aircraft. Switches make and break those joins by hand; relays and contactors make and break them electrically. Every aircraft from a two-seat trainer to a widebody uses one of these three layouts, and the choice is a trade between simplicity, fault containment and redundancy.
prereq: You need: 3.1 for generation and protection, 3.9 for the regulator that sets each generator's voltage, and 3.10 for the breakers that feed each load.

blocks.text: A busbar is a thick copper or aluminium bar. It collects power from one or more sources and hands it to a group of loads. Copper is common; aluminium saves weight on long runs. The bar is sized so its resistance, and the volt drop along it, stay small.

A split bus (also called an isolated bus) gives each generator its own bar. Generator 1 closes onto bus 1 through its generator circuit breaker (GCB), a heavy-duty contactor that the GCU closes and trips; Airbus calls the same device the generator line contactor. Generator 2 closes onto bus 2 through its own GCB. The two busbars never touch.

The gain is fault containment. A short on bus 1 trips GCB 1 and the aircraft loses bus 1 only. Nothing needs synchronising, because no two generators are ever connected to the same bar; a battery or a TRU may share a bus with a generator, but two generators never do. The wiring between the halves stays light and the control logic stays simple.

The price is that a generator failure strands its bus. Its DC loads can then be carried by the battery (see 3.3) or by a TRU fed from the other side's AC bus (see 3.2), but the AC loads of that side are lost unless a tie is closed. A single-engine aircraft is the simplest case: one generator, one main bus, a battery bus and an essential bus tapped off it. A light twin has one generator per engine on a common or split DC bus.

On a parallel bus all generators close onto one bar. Before a GCB closes, the incoming generator's voltage must match the bus; on AC, frequency and phase must match as well. That is the synchronism check, done by a synchroscope or by an automatic paralleling unit. Closing out of phase drives a large circulating current through both machines.
Once closed, the machines stay in step and share the load. Sharing is not arranged by setting exactly equal no-load voltages. Real machines have droop: terminal voltage falls as current rises.

blocks.where: V is the terminal voltage in volts, V₀ is the no-load voltage in volts, k is the droop coefficient in volts per ampere, and I is the generator current in amperes.

blocks.text: Two generators on one bus must sit at the same terminal voltage, so for equal no-load voltages the one with the smaller k takes the larger current. With unequal no-load voltages, solve V₀ − kI for both machines. Deliberate droop of a few percent from no-load to full load makes sharing predictable and stable. A load controller can also trim field currents to equalise the share. On AC systems the constant-speed drive holds frequency at 400 Hz, the engine governor sets kilowatt sharing, and the regulator sets reactive sharing.

Split-parallel is the normal state of most twin-engine transports. The buses are split and each generator carries its own side, so fault containment is kept. A bus tie breaker, written BTB, sits between the two buses and stays open in normal flight.

When one generator drops offline its GCB opens and the BTB closes, so the surviving generator feeds both buses. Non-essential loads — galleys, cabin sockets, entertainment — must be shed first, because one generator is rarely rated for the whole aircraft load. A bus power control unit can do this automatically after a short delay.

Normal flight behaves like a split bus; a failure behaves like a parallel bus. An essential bus can also be fed from both sides through diodes, which pass current from either main bus into the essential bus but never from one main bus to the other, so the open BTB is not bypassed and the essential bus keeps power whichever side survives.

Cockpit switches are worked by hand: the toggle switch, which stays where it is set; the push-button, which is often momentary and springs back; and the rotary selector, with many positions. Two other switches are worked by the aircraft itself: the microswitch, a tiny snap-action switch pressed by a lever or strut as a limit switch on a door or the landing gear, and the proximity switch, a non-contact sensor that detects a metal target and reports gear up or down.

A relay is an electrically operated switch. A small current in the coil makes a magnetic field that pulls the armature and moves the contacts. Normally open (NO) contacts close when the coil is energised; normally closed (NC) contacts open. A latching relay holds its last state with no coil current. A contactor is a heavy-duty relay for busbars and generators — same principle, bigger contacts, with arc quenching.

A contact rating must cover the making and breaking current, not only the steady current. A DC coil needs a suppression diode across it: when the coil is switched off, its inductance drives a large reverse voltage that would pit the controlling contacts. The diode gives that stored energy a path. A solid-state power controller (SSPC) replaces the relay with a MOSFET plus current sensing, so it can control and protect the wire in one device (see 3.10).

examples.question: Two 28 V DC generators run in parallel on a 300 A bus load. Each has a no-load voltage of 28.5 V. Generator 1 droops 0.4 V per 100 A and generator 2 droops 0.6 V per 100 A. Find the current in each generator and the bus voltage.
steps: Convert each droop to volts per ampere: k₁ = 0.4 ÷ 100 = 0.004 V/A and k₂ = 0.6 ÷ 100 = 0.006 V/A.
In parallel the terminal voltages are equal: 28.5 − 0.004 I₁ = 28.5 − 0.006 I₂.
Cancel the 28.5 V on both sides: 0.004 I₁ = 0.006 I₂, so I₁ = 1.5 I₂.
The load must balance the two currents: I₁ + I₂ = 300 A, so 1.5 I₂ + I₂ = 2.5 I₂ = 300 A, giving I₂ = 120 A.
Check on generator 2: 28.5 − 0.006 × 120 = 28.5 − 0.72 = 27.78 V. The two agree.
examples.answer: Generator 1 carries 180 A, generator 2 carries 120 A, and the bus voltage is 27.78 V.

traps: Assuming parallel generators must have exactly equal no-load voltages. They share by droop, so equal set points with unequal slopes still give unequal currents.
Paralleling AC generators without a synchronism check. Closing out of phase gives a huge circulating current and can damage the drive.
Confusing the generator circuit breaker (GCB) with the bus tie breaker (BTB): the GCB joins one generator to its own bus, the BTB joins the two buses.
Treating a split bus as redundancy. It contains faults, but a lost generator leaves its DC loads on the battery or a TRU and its AC loads dead, until a tie is closed.
Leaving out the suppression diode across a DC relay coil, so the inductive kickback pits the controlling switch contacts.

quiz.q: What is a busbar, and why is it made thick?
quiz.a: A copper or aluminium bar that distributes power from sources to a group of loads. It is thick so its resistance and volt drop stay small.

quiz.q: State two differences between a relay and a contactor.
quiz.a: A contactor is built for heavy currents (busbars, generators) with large contacts and arc quenching; a relay is a small control device. Both work on the same coil-and-armature principle.

quiz.q: Why does a split bus need no synchronising, while a parallel bus does?
quiz.a: On a split bus no two generators are ever on the same bar, so there is nothing to match. On a parallel bus two generators join one bar, so their voltages must match, and for AC their frequency and phase too.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a suppression diode across a DC relay coil?
quiz.a: When the coil current is interrupted, the coil's inductance drives a large reverse voltage. The diode gives that stored energy a circulating path, protecting the switch or transistor that drives the coil.

quiz.q: Two 28.5 V no-load generators run in parallel on a 250 A load. Generator 1 droops 0.2 V per 100 A and generator 2 droops 0.3 V per 100 A. Find each current and the bus voltage.
quiz.a: k₁ = 0.002 V/A, k₂ = 0.003 V/A. Equal terminal volts give 0.002 I₁ = 0.003 I₂, so I₁ = 1.5 I₂. With I₁ + I₂ = 250 A, I₂ = 100 A and I₁ = 150 A. Bus voltage = 28.5 − 0.002 × 150 = 28.2 V.

quiz.q: After one generator fails on a split-parallel aircraft, why must non-essential loads be shed before the bus tie breaker closes?
quiz.a: The surviving generator is rated for its own bus, not for the whole aircraft load. Closing the tie onto the full load would overload it and trip its protection, leaving both buses dead. Shedding galleys and cabin loads brings the demand inside one generator's rating.

quiz.q: Why does split-parallel operation give both fault containment and redundancy, which neither pure split nor pure parallel gives?
quiz.a: In normal flight the tie is open, so a fault on one bus trips only that side's GCB: that is fault containment. After a generator failure the tie closes and the other generator feeds both sides: that is redundancy. Pure split has no backup for a lost generator; pure parallel lets one bus fault pull down every generator at once.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern transports replace relay logic with solid-state power controllers that report current, trip on overcurrent and detect arc faults in the same package, so the busbar is monitored load by load. High-voltage DC architectures at 270 V DC need contactors that break DC arcs, and variable-frequency AC needs electronic real and reactive load sharing because there is no constant-speed drive. Search for 'bus power control unit', 'solid-state power controller' and 'arc fault circuit breaker' to go further.

figure.caption: Left: split-parallel layout. Each generator feeds its own bus through its GCB; the bus tie breaker (BTB) stays open in normal flight, and the essential bus is fed through diodes from either side, with the battery as standby. Right: the worked example's droop lines meet the common 27.78 V at 180 A (GEN 1) and 120 A (GEN 2).
